# Why percentages, not dollars? {.divider background-color="#008CB7"}

[Act I · The tension]{.act}

## Economists care about *proportionate* change

A \$10,000 raise means very different things at a \$30,000 salary and at a \$300,000 salary.

. . .

So the number we usually want is a **percentage**, not a dollar amount — a return to education, a price
elasticity, a growth rate. The natural logarithm is the one transformation that turns a regression slope
directly into that percentage.

::: {.notes}
Economic theory is overwhelmingly about proportionate responses: elasticities of demand, percentage
returns, growth rates. Logs let OLS speak that language without changing the estimator.
:::

## Where we're going

::: {.incremental}
- **One property** of $\ln$ that makes it the workhorse of econometrics
- **Semi-elasticity vs elasticity** — the two ways $y$ can respond to $x$
- **Four functional forms** (level, log-linear, log-log, linear-log) and how each slope is read
- **Earnings & education** — the same data, four interpretations, with `pyfixest`
- **Exponential growth** — logs linearize it, and the Rule of 72 reads off a doubling time
:::

## Five ideas anchor this chapter

::: {.incremental}
- **Natural log $\ln$** — inverse of $e^x$; turns *multiplicative* differences into *additive* ones
- **Key approximation** — $\Delta \ln(x) \approx \Delta x / x$, so $100 \times \Delta\ln(x) \approx \%\Delta x$
- **Semi-elasticity** — $\%\Delta y$ per **one-unit** change in $x$ (log-linear slope)
- **Elasticity** — $\%\Delta y$ per **1%** change in $x$ (log-log slope), unit-free
- **Compound growth** — $x_t = x_0(1+r)^t$ is a straight line once you log it
:::

[Logs let a single regression slope be read as a percentage — that is the whole point.]{.takeaway .fragment}

# From logs to elasticities {.divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Act II · The investigation]{.act}

## The one log property that matters: $\Delta \ln(x) \approx \Delta x / x$

For *small* changes, the change in $\ln(x)$ *is* the proportionate change in $x$ — multiply by 100 to get a percent.

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-4|6-9"}
import numpy as np                           # numpy → logs, exponentials, arrays

x0, x1 = 40, 40.4                            # x rises from 40 to 40.4 (a 1% increase)

exact  = (x1 - x0) / x0                      # exact proportionate change = 0.010000
approx = np.log(x1) - np.log(x0)             # log approximation Δln(x)   = 0.009950
print(f"exact proportionate change: {exact:.6f}  ({exact*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"log approximation Δln(x):   {approx:.6f}  ({approx*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"difference: {abs(exact-approx):.6f}")   # tiny — the approximation is excellent for small moves
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
numpy (preinstalled in Colab) is all we need here. The gap between 1.0000% and 0.9950% is the
approximation error — negligible under ~10%, which is exactly why logs are so convenient.
:::

## Two responses: semi-elasticity vs elasticity

::: {.incremental}
- **Semi-elasticity** $= \dfrac{\Delta y / y}{\Delta x}$ — a **one-unit** move in $x$ (e.g. one more year of school) → a percentage move in $y$. Estimated by a **log-linear** slope.
- **Elasticity** $= \dfrac{\Delta y / y}{\Delta x / x}$ — a **1%** move in $x$ → a percentage move in $y$. Unit-free. Estimated by a **log-log** slope.
:::

| Form | Model | Slope $\beta_1$ reads as |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ | $\Delta y$ in units per unit of $x$ |
| Log-linear | $\ln y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ | $100\beta_1 \approx \%\Delta y$ per unit of $x$ |
| Log-log | $\ln y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln x$ | $\beta_1 = $ elasticity (% per %) |
| Linear-log | $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln x$ | $\beta_1/100 = \Delta y$ per 1% of $x$ |

## Our question: how do earnings vary with education?

171 full-time women workers aged 30 (2010). Earnings are **right-skewed** (mean \$41,413, median \$36,000, max \$172,000),
so the log scale pulls in the long tail. We take logs and fit all four forms with `pyfixest`.

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-5|7-9|11-15|17-18"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                     # pyfixest is NOT preinstalled in Colab (-q = quiet)

import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
import numpy as np                           # np.log for the transforms
import pyfixest as pf                        # OLS with R-style formulas

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_EARNINGS.DTA"
data = pd.read_stata(url)                    # 171 women aged 30: earnings, education
data["lnearn"] = np.log(data["earnings"])    # log of the outcome
data["lneduc"] = np.log(data["education"].astype(float))   # log of the regressor (int8 → float first)

m_lin    = pf.feols("earnings ~ education", data=data)   # 1. linear:      $ per year
m_loglin = pf.feols("lnearn ~ education",   data=data)   # 2. log-linear:  semi-elasticity
m_loglog = pf.feols("lnearn ~ lneduc",      data=data)   # 3. log-log:     elasticity
m_linlog = pf.feols("earnings ~ lneduc",    data=data)   # 4. linear-log:  $ per 1%

print(100 * m_loglin.coef()["education"])    # 13.1 → ~13.1% more earnings per extra year
m_loglin.summary()                           # β0, β1, SE, t, p, R²
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
The log-linear model is the labor-economics default: the 13.1% return scales automatically — it reads
the same whether a worker earns \$30k or \$100k. t = 9.21, p < 0.001, R² = 0.334.
:::

## Same data, four fitted lines — four different questions

![Each panel fits one specification. The log transforms straighten the curvature the linear model misses.](figures/fig_four_models.png)

[Log-linear fits best among the $\ln$(earnings) models (R² = 0.334); logging only $x$ bends the line into diminishing returns.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Reading the four slopes

::: {.incremental}
- **Linear:** \$5,021 more earnings per extra year — a fixed dollar amount (implausible at the top end).
- **Log-linear:** about **13.1% more** earnings per extra year — the semi-elasticity, and the usual choice.
- **Log-log:** elasticity **1.48** — a 1% rise in education is associated with ~1.48% higher earnings.
- **Linear-log:** about **\$545 more** earnings per 1% of education — dollars from a percentage move.
:::

[Compare $R^2$ only across models with the **same** dependent variable — not across level and log outcomes.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Exponential growth becomes a straight line in logs

$x_t = x_0(1+r)^t$ curves upward in levels, but $\ln(x_t) = \ln(x_0) + \ln(1+r)\,t \approx \ln(x_0) + r\,t$ is linear — so the slope of
$\ln x$ on time estimates $\ln(1+r) \approx r$; the exact rate is $e^{\text{slope}} - 1$.

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-5|7-8|10|11-14"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                     # self-contained cell: install pyfixest (quiet)

import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
import numpy as np                           # np.exp for the exact growth rate
import pyfixest as pf                        # OLS with R-style formulas

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_SP500INDEX.DTA"
data = pd.read_stata(url)                    # S&P 500 index, 1927–2019 (lnsp500 precomputed)

fit = pf.feols("lnsp500 ~ year", data=data)  # slope = ln(1+r) ≈ growth rate r
r = fit.coef()["year"]                       # ≈ 0.0653
print(f"log slope: {100*r:.2f}% per year")   # ≈ 6.53% (log approximation)
print(f"exact growth: {100*(np.exp(r)-1):.2f}% per year")   # ≈ 6.75% per year
print(f"Rule of 72: doubles every {72/(100*r):.0f} years")  # ≈ 11 years
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
lnsp500 is already in the dataset. The Rule of 72 comes from ln(2) ≈ 0.693 and ln(1+r) ≈ r: divide 72
by the percentage rate for an instant doubling time.
:::

## Logs turn a curve into a slope you can read

![The same S&P 500 series: an exponential curve in levels (left), a near-straight line in logs (right).](figures/fig_exp_growth.png)

[Log slope **0.065** → exact growth of about **6.75% per year** over 1927–2019 → the index doubles about every **11 years** (Rule of 72).]{.takeaway .fragment}

# Reading it right {.divider background-color="#C21E72"}

[Act III · The resolution]{.act}

## The approximation has limits — and logs have a domain

[Objection.]{.objection} "The log-linear slope is 0.131, so the return to a year of education is exactly 13.1%."

. . .

[Response.]{.rebuttal} $100\beta_1$ is an **approximation** that holds for small coefficients. At $\beta_1 = 0.131$
the *exact* effect is $100\,(e^{0.131}-1) \approx 14.0\%$ — close, but not identical. And $\ln$ is undefined at
zero or negative values, so logs only apply to strictly positive variables.

[Report the exact $100(e^{\beta_1}-1)$ once $|\beta_1|$ clears about 0.10; never log a variable that can be zero.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## What to carry forward

::: {.incremental}
- $\Delta\ln(x) \approx \Delta x/x$: a log change **is** a proportionate change (for small moves).
- **Log-linear** → semi-elasticity ($100\beta_1 \approx \%\Delta y$ per unit); **log-log** → elasticity (% per %).
- Choose the form from **economic theory + data + interpretation** — log-linear is the common default.
- **Exponential growth is linear in logs**: regress $\ln x$ on time; the slope estimates $\ln(1+r) \approx r$ (exact: $e^{\text{slope}} - 1$).
- Treat finite percentage effects as **approximations** ($100(e^{\beta_1}-1)$ is exact); logs need positive data.
:::
